utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the interpreters, the staff of the audiovisual booth, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. Case number IT-98-30-T, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mladjo Radic, and Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Prosecutor, can we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleague Mr. Waidyaratne, and assisting the Prosecution today is Ms. Reynders and Mr. Saxon. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. For the Defence, can we have the appearances, please, in the order in which the accused are listed in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Krstan Simic. With me is Mr. Branko Lukic, co-counsel. Together we represent Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. I take advantage of the occasion to welcome your co-counsel. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of the accused Milojica Kos consists of Mrs. Jelena Nikolic, legal counsel; Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, co-counsel; and myself, Zarko Nikolic, as lead counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Zoran Jovanovic and myself represent the Defence counsel for Mr. Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm attorney Tosic representing Mr. Zoran Zigic. To my left is my co-counsel Mr. Slobodan Stojanovic, attorney from Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I say good morning to all the co-counsel who are here in the hall for the first time. Good morning also to the public. For the benefit of the public in the gallery, I wish to tell you that we are at the beginning of the trial, according to our Rules, this is Rule 84. That is to say, we are going to have the opening statement of the Prosecutor, which will be followed by the testimony of the accused, Mr. Kvocka, Mr. Kos, and Mr. Radic. Today we are going to have the opening statement by the Prosecutor, and tomorrow we'll have the testimony of Mr. Kvocka. So I now give the floor to Mr. Niemann for your opening statement. Please, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours, please. Your Honours, during the course of my presentation here today, I'll be referring to a number of documentary exhibits which, as I refer to them, will appear on Your Honours' television screen, and the section that Your Honours will see is the essence of the document that I seek to refer to in the course of this opening. These documents have been provided to the Defence, some of which they've had for some considerable time. And some of the documents, in fact all of them except one, has formally been admitted by order of the previous Trial Chamber. In order to facilitate a smooth demonstration of these documents and other material, might I have Your Honours' leave for Ms. Reynders and Mr. Saxon to sit here near the machine so that the documents can be placed on the machine as I refer to them. Thank you, Your Honours. I also have had prepared, Your Honours, three binders of documents which are not in the nature of exhibits as such. They are, in fact, copies of what are the exhibits and what will be tendered in the course of the proceedings, but they are the documents that I will refer to, and they're placed in the order that I will refer to them. Your Honours, these I hand to you, and I ask the registrar if he would hand them to you so that you could refer to them if you wish or, alternatively, if you want to see the whole document or later refer to it, it is there for that purpose. But for the most part, Your Honours need not do that unless you want to, because as I say, it will appear on the screen and at the same time I will read the contents of the document to you. So I'm not asking you to follow it religiously, but it's there for your convenience if that is of assistance to Your Honours. So perhaps they could be handed up. Oh, I see that Your Honours have them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor. You may continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, this trial is about a government policy of persecution and ethnic cleansing. The crime was on a massive scale. The who, when, where, why, and how of the crime illustrates its dimension. If we pose these questions, we begin to see the scope of this criminal activity. Who committed the crime? Well, it was certainly committed by more people than you have here before you today. It consisted of a large number of politicians, police, and military leaders, and loyal followers of the Republika Srpska. It was this puppet entity, dangling from the strings of Slobodan Milosevic, that turned its police and military forces upon its own people in a quest to participate in the grand achievement of an ethnically pure Greater Serbia. When was the crime committed? It was committed from about April of 1992, and to some extent, the ramifications of that crime are still felt by the victims today. But what happened in April - May of 1992 was not some random unexpected event. It was a well-planned, orchestrated campaign of terror that had been in the making for some considerable time. Where was it committed? It was committed across a large swathe of Bosnia-Herzegovina but mostly the areas to the north of Sarajevo and particularly in the Bosnian-Serb dominated areas to the north and west of that republic. Why was it committed? It was committed because a handful of ethnocentric fanatical nationalists had seized power and were intent on forcing their nationalistic fanaticism on the whole of the population. How was it committed? It was committed by subjecting the non-Serbian, mostly Bosnian Muslim and Croat population of the area to the most savage, brutal, and inhumane campaign of terror, the likes of which have not been witnessed in Europe since the end of World War II. This trial is about this campaign of wholesale persecution of Bosnian Muslims and Croat populations at the hands of the Bosnian Serbs and how the accused before you participated in this campaign of persecution and terror. To understand these crimes, it's not possible to close our eyes to the wider nature of the crime and nor is it proper for us to do so. These are not just crimes of murder, rape, and beating. First and foremost, they are crimes of a policy of persecution unleashed by a state on its civilian population. It occurred during an armed conflict and was committed on a widespread and systematic basis. Fortunately, Your Honours do not have to trouble yourselves with domestic murders, rapes, and beatings that may have occurred in Bosnia at the time. You only become concerned when the murders, rapes, and beatings, and the like were committed in furtherance of this crime of persecution. Nor do Your Honours have jurisdiction to try states for the crimes that they might commit, but it is the individuals employed by the state to commit the crimes over whom your jurisdiction lies. The bulk of the evidence that you will hear will describe three prison camps in north-western Bosnia which operated during the spring and summer of 1992 as instruments of this policy, and the acts and omissions of the four accused who were responsible directly or indirectly for many of the atrocities that occurred in those camps. The evidence will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that thousands of Muslims and Croat detainees suffered and died at those prison camps because of their ethnicity, either directly at the hands of the accused or at the hands of individuals who were subject to the defendants' authority. These accused may well try to impress upon you that it was not them who planned, instigated, or ordered this campaign of persecution and terror, but that it is something that came from above, and to some extent that might be so. But how does a state commit a crime? A state has no mind, it has no physical possibilities. It is the servants of the state that make it function, or, in this case, dysfunction. This discriminatory campaign of persecution, this criminal enterprise, was given birth to by the human instruments of the state, and it was these accused who joined this criminal enterprise. As I said a moment ago, throughout this presentation, I'm going to refer to a number of documents that were seized by investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor during the execution of search warrants in Prijedor and the city of Banja Luka. As I describe each of those documents, they will appear on Your Honours' screens. First, the first page of the document will appear as a whole, and the precise extract that I'm reading from will then become visible. Your Honours, prior to 1992, the municipality of Prijedor was a multiethnic, relatively peaceful region. The total population of Prijedor municipality was approximately 112.000 persons. About 50.000 were Muslim, 48.000 were Serbs, 6000 were Croats, and the remainder identified themselves as Yugoslavs or other nationalities. When the Bosnian Serb persecution campaign ended, only 6.000 Muslims and 3.000 Croats remained in Prijedor, living, according to the Bosnian Serbs' own assessment, in permanent fear and uncertainty. The creation and operation of the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps were part of the Bosnian Serb plan to ethnically cleanse the Prijedor municipality of non-Serbs. Bosnian Serb leaders targeted ethnic Muslims and ethnic Croats for persecution, particularly intellectuals and politicians who could impede their efforts to create a Greater Serbia. Your Honours, persecution consists of a severe attack on fundamental human rights, with the aim of excluding the victim from society on discriminatory grounds. The evidence presented during this trial will prove that these accused and others under their supervision confined, beat, tortured, sexually assaulted, and murdered many of the Muslim and Croat detainees at the prison camps during the summer of 1992 solely because of the victims' ethnicity. Your Honours, images of skeletal malnourished people at the detention camps in Prijedor sent shock waves around the world when they were first broadcast in 1992. Allow the Prosecution to share some of this video footage with you. Your Honours, we have a short clip of video that I'd now ask to be played. The first segment of the video shows Radovan Karadzic in his mountain headquarters in Pale, speaking to Western journalists, where he emphatically denies the existence of civilian camps. The second segment is taken shortly after this interview, when the journalists finally gained permission to visit these camps. Their visit is delayed as the worst of the detainees are moved out, some to Trnopolje and others to Manjaca. But fortunately, Western media caught up with these detainees who were mostly being held at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is when conditions were good, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting. Can the accused follow the pictures? Mr. Registrar, will you please help us with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, I might ask the technicians if they can roll back to the beginning of the tape and play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Niemann, excuse me, but we have a technical problem, and therefore I think we will have to make a break of at least ten minutes for the problem to be fixed and for the accused to be able to see the video pictures. So we'll have a ten-minute break. --- Break taken at 10.55 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that everything is in order now. Mr. Prosecutor, we apologise for this interruption. Please continue your opening statement now, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I think because that video segment was interrupted, I'd like to play it again, if I may. It's very short anyway. So could I ask the technical booth if they could play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the establishment of these camps. In late May 1992, Bosnian Serb authorities established a prison camp at the Omarska mine, located to the south-east of the town of Prijedor. Simo Drljaca was the chief of police at Prijedor in May of 1992. He was indicted by this Tribunal for, among other things, crimes arising out of some of the same incidences that the accused before you today have been charged. Simo Drljaca was the superior of the accused Kvocka, Radic, and Kos. In July of 1997, an attempt was made by SFOR to affect his arrest, but during the course of his arrest, Drljaca drew a pistol. Shots were fired, which resulted in his being fatally shot, but not before a young British soldier was injured. Well, this very same Simo Drljaca issued an order, on the 31st of May of 1992, in his capacity as the chief of police in Prijedor. In this order, he explains the new purpose of the mine at Omarska. If we could now have that document on the screen, please. Your Honours, in the first paragraph of this document, Simo Drljaca says that: "The industrial compound of the Omarska strip mine shall serve as a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the security services' operational information." We're not told, Your Honours, what security services operational information means, but I suggest to you that by the conclusion of the Prosecution evidence, Your Honours will have a clear understanding of the meaning of that euphemistic phrase. In the second paragraph he says: "Together with the appropriate documents, the persons taken into custody shall be handed over to the chief of security, who is duty-bound, in collaboration with the national, public, and military security coordinator, to put them up in any of the five premises allocated for accommodation of detainees." Well, Your Honours, you will see the conditions that were provided for the so-called accommodation of detainees, and I'm sure that you will see that they were far from adequate. Then in paragraph 3 he says: "A mixed group consisting of national, public, and military security investigators shall be responsible for the work with and categorisation of detainees. They shall organise themselves respecting the parity principle and Mirko Jesic, Ranko Mujic, and the Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic shall be responsible for the work." Going on to paragraph 6, he says in this order that: "Security services at the collection centre shall be provided by the Omarska police station with an adequate number of policemen who shall be present at the collection centre at all times and shall organise guard duty according to the on duty-on call-off duty principle." Your Honours, the accused Kvocka and Radic came from the Omarska police station, as did the commander of the camp, Zeljko Meakic. In paragraph 8, he says: "The management shall, without delay, fence off the compound around the management building with barbed wire, placing a barrier on the road to Omarska and shall also provide drinking water. The guards shall prevent any unauthorised persons from approaching or entering the collection centre in accordance with the official guard-duty rules." Then in paragraph 9: "Authorised representatives of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall without delay lay a minefield in accordance with mining regulations, which includes making a minefield layout, correct markings, etc." The significance of these paragraphs, Your Honour, is that clearly there was no difficulty in controlling who was kept in the camp, but similarly, there was absolutely no difficulty at all in controlling who entered the camp. Then finally, in paragraph 11: "The security services coordinators shall submit a report on the preceding 24 hours to the Chief of the Prijedor Public Security Station daily at 12.00 hours or immediately when the circumstances allow no delay." And finally paragraph 15: "I most strictly prohibit giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre. All official documents shall be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the Chief of the Prijedor Public Security Station. This shall be the responsibility of the security staff." From this document, Your Honours, we see that there is no question that the information went up the command and down and that it was kept highly confidential and for obvious reasons. Officially, Omarska was meant to serve as a temporary detention service for prisoners of war but most of the detainees were Muslim and Croat civilians. Omarska held many prominent Muslim intellectuals, academics, businessmen, and politicians. The Bosnian Serb authorities called Omarska a "collection centre." However, the evidence will prove beyond reasonable doubt that Omarska was a prison camp and an interrogation centre, a place where murder, torture, rape, and other cruel and inhumane treatment were a daily occurrence. The prison guards, mostly policemen from the Omarska substation, like the accused Kvocka, Radic, and Kos, committed many of these crimes. Every part of the Omarska facility used to detain prisoners was overcrowded. Open space was so limited that in some instances prisoners could not even sit or lie down. Detainees could not move at all unless they received permission explicitly to use the toilet or to eat. Often guards beat them savagely on their way to use the toilet, so many preferred to defecate in their clothing rather than to risk this treatment. The prison camp did not supply bedding or prisoners often used their clothing as pillows or covers. Although the weather was very hot during the summer of 1992, the prisoners received very little water. The water they did receive was often unsanitary and often the prisoners became ill as a result. Prisoners had no opportunity to maintain their personal hygiene and lice, dysentery, and other water-borne diseases were commonplace at Omarska. If I might direct Your Honours' attention to the model that is before you here, and perhaps I might ask the assistance of Ms. Reynders to come forward and point out some of the features of the model as it appears. Your Honour will see that there are four main buildings which are used as part of the prison camp. The administration building, the hangar building, the building that's referred to as the White House, the Red House, and the pista. Thank you. Each building had its own role in the functioning of the camp. The administration centre, for example, housed a kitchen and a canteen on the ground floor where the prisoners were allowed only a few minutes to eat. They were given starvation rations to survive on, consisting of soup and a tiny piece of bread. Some of the prisoners lost as much as 20 to 30 kilograms of weight in the period of one to three months. Also, the ground floor was a large room where certain prisoners were held, and also a small garage where prisoners were kept. Could I please ask that the photographs of the administration area be shown. This building we're now looking at is an area of the administration building where prisoners were kept. Your Honours, on the first floor of the administration building there are eight rooms used for the daily interrogation of the prisoners. Those offices were also used for the administration of the camp and the sleeping quarters for the nearly 40 female prisoners held at the camp. These women were forced to clean the inspection rooms every day, and the walls and floors of the room that they scrubbed were often covered with blood, hair, skin, and teeth, and the grotesque by-products of what the authorities euphemistically referred to as "processing" the prisoners. Many of the female detainees were raped or otherwise sexually assault on a nightly basis in the administration area. Typically, a guard would come to the women's room and would call out to one or two of them and take them to a guard or camp official who then often raped and beat them. The accused Mladjo Radic, also known as Krkan, is so charged in the indictment. The pista. Between the canteen and the hangar was a L-shaped, 30-metre long slab of cement known as the "pista". When the prisoners ate, they were forced to run across the pista to and from the canteen, where they were subjected to beatings as they ran. Often the detainees had to run a gauntlet through a cordon of guards to beat them with rifle butts, batons, fists, and boots. Many prisoners were also left out in the open on the pista regardless of the weather conditions. It was on the pista where Slavko Ecimovic, the leader of the Prijedor's Muslim community, was brutally beaten in front of a number of other prisoners in June of 1992. Before he was captured by Serb forces, Mr. Ecimovic let a group of poorly armed Muslim fighters in an abortive, perhaps Quixotic attempt to capture the town of Prijedor. Mr. Ecimovic was beaten by a group of guards who shouted to the other prisoners, "Here is your leader. Here is your Ustashe. Look at him." At the time, Mr. Ecimovic had his hands tied behind his back and both of his cheeks had been punctured with barbed wire. The hangar building. During peacetime, the hangar building held the trucks and machinery of the iron ore mine. But when the mine served as a prisoner camp, the bulk of the prisoners at Omarska were housed in this hangar building. I think, Your Honours, if I may ask for assistance, we have a photograph here of the inside of that very building, and Your Honours can see there the equipment that was used. Hardly a suitable place, you might think, for the keeping of prisoners during times of war. Staircases were often used as places where people were kept as well, and they had to live in these conditions. On the ground floor there was a room where many prisoners were held, and the first floor, which was smaller than the ground floor, also held some detainees. The White House. Before the armed conflict, the White House was used as a first-aid station for injured miners. Ironically, it was in this very same White House that the prisoners detain at Omarska received the most brutal treatment and were often murdered. Normally those marked for special treatment were those considered to be extremists by the Serbs, such as civic leaders or members of the SDA, the Muslim political party. With the exception of one woman, only male prisoners were kept in the White House. During this trial, you will hear testimony that it was in the White House that the accused Zoran Zigic and others brutally beat Becir Medunjanin over a two-day period. Becir Medunjanin was the president of the SDA, and witnesses will testify that he received particularly harsh treatment due to his prominent position in the Muslim community. The Red House. The last of the four buildings in the compound, the Red House, was used as a work utility room when the Omarska mine was operational. When the mine was converted for use as a prison camp, prisoners who entered the Red House were rarely ever seen again. The disposal of the bodies. Just about every morning during the relevant period of indictment, at least five to ten bodies, and often more, were piled upon each other outside of the White House to be carried away in trucks. The Serbs buried many of these bodies at the remnants of a village of Kevljani, a Muslim village located four kilometres from the Omarska prison camp, which was destroyed by Serb forces during the ethnic cleansing campaign. The bodies were dumped into a series of graves dug into a meadow adjoining the flattened mosque that once stood in Kevljani. We dug up that grave. Personnel from the Office of the Prosecutor exhumed 72 bodies from these graves, but the evidence presented during trial will prove that an undetermined number of bodies were removed from these graves prior to the OTP's exhumation. If I might ask that some of the photos of the exhumation be shown at this stage. Many of the bodies found in the exhumation will demonstrate that the injuries received, in many cases, were blunt-object injury and bullet wounds. The next one, please. The next one, please. This poor unfortunate individual had modern keys. Many of them were buried with their clothes on. Many of them, as I said, had gunshot wounds in the head. And modern artefacts were found in the grave. Thank you. With the assistance of DNA analysis, the Prosecution has reliably identified several of the bodies unearthed at Kevljani as former prisoners of the Omarska camp. The closing of the camp. The Bosnian Serb authorities in Prijedor operated the camp at Omarska until early August of 1992. When the international press discovered the camp and the horrific conditions existing there, the international media exposure forced the Serbs to curtail their criminal activity at Omarska, and most of the prisoners were transferred to other prison camps at Trnopolje and Manjaca. Many prisoners were beaten or killed during these so-called transfers. In a dispatch, dated August the 5th, 1992, Simo Drljaca, who I referred to early, the chief of police for Prijedor, described in clinical terms the results of the so-called processing of prisoners in Omarska. Could we have the next document, please. In this report, he says: "Please be advised that the Prijedor Public Security Station, in cooperation with the competent security services of the Banja Luka CSB and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, has completed the processing of the prisoners of war. "The investigation has found elements of criminal activity in 1.466 cases, for which valid documentation exists, which we shall transfer under guard, along with the persons it pertains to, to the Manjaca military camp on 6 August 1992. The remaining persons are of no security interest and will be transferred to the reception camp in Trnopolje on the same day and under escort provided by the SJB. Trnopolje is a location where Muslims fleeing from the combat operations in the municipality found shelter. Security at the camp is provided by the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Well, Your Honours, the evidence will demonstrate clearly the nature of the so-called crimes and nature of the so-called prisoners of war to which he refers. When the prisoners were removed from Omarska on August 6th, 1992, some of the transferees were killed or otherwise disappeared. Approximately 80 prisoners in relatively good health remained behind in the camp to create the public facade that nothing was amiss. And what could be described as being "in relatively good health" was the photographs that Your Honours saw of the man eating in the Omarska camp. Subsequently, those prisoners left behind were also transferred to the prison camps at Trnopolje and Manjaca, and hundreds were killed at a remote area called Vlasic Mountain on the 21st of August, 1992. On 23 August 1992, Simo Drljaca reported to his superiors in Banja Luka about these prisoners who had been transferred to Manjaca. Could I have the next document, please. We see in this reporter here: "We are hereby informing you that the required documentation concerning the prisoners of war who have been transferred from Omarska Investigation Centre to Manjaca prisoner-of-war camp was forwarded to the commander of the Manjaca prisoners-of-war camp today." And we can see those prisoners in the photograph that Your Honours will see on the screen now, if we could have the photograph now, please, of the detainees as they were kept in the Manjaca so-called prisoners-of-war camp. Thank you. Thus, the police in the Prijedor municipality were involved at every stage of the persecution campaign directed at the Muslims and Croats. The Bosnian Serb police were so sure of their power as well as their righteousness of their cause that they kept accurate records about their criminal activity. The Keraterm camp. The Keraterm ceramics factory served as another important component of the Serb persecution campaign in Prijedor. On May 25th, 1992, the factory became a fully operational detention centre, holding some 2.000 to 3.000 prisoners. Most of the detainees were Muslim and Croat men from the Prijedor region. They were kept in four rooms, under conditions so crowded that often they could not lie down or move about, and again were fed starvation rations. Could we please have the photograph of the Keraterm facility. This is a photograph showing the front of a building and a building known as the "weigh bridge," which guards often used during the time that Keraterm became a prison camp. Thank you. As one of the complexes of prison camps for Muslims and Croats in the Prijedor region, Keraterm was an important part of the common Serb plan to ethnically cleanse Prijedor of non-Serbs. All of the detainees in Keraterm were subjected to mistreatment, such as murder, beatings, rapes, and macabre and sadistic acts of torture. The Bosnian Serbs often committed these degradations in full view of other prisoners so as to magnify the horror and humiliation of the detainees, and thereby break their spirit. No medical attention was offered to the detainees, even after they had been savagely beaten. Corpses of prisoners were often piled inside the detention rooms or adjacent to a trash bin at the end of the factory, near Room 4. The camp guards forced the surviving detainees to carry the bodies outdoors and load them onto trucks. It was in Keraterm, during mid July of 1992, where the accused Zoran Zigic, together with certain camp guards, brutally beat many prisoners, including Jasmin Izeiri, Spija Mesic, and Drago Tokmadzic, in front of the detention rooms. It was in Keraterm, during late July of 1992, where we allege that the accused Zoran Zigic and others severely beat a group of prisoners, including Emsud Bahonjic and a man named Sead Jusufagic, known by the nickname "Car," over a period of several days. Emsud Bahonjic became blind as a result of the beating, his limbs were broken, and he died an agonising and cruel death. Mr. Zigic and others subjected detainees to violent and degrading acts, such as being forced to lie on broken glass and to commit fellatio with other male prisoners. Furthermore, it was at Keraterm camp during June of 1992 where the accused Zoran Zigic and others brutally beat Fajzo Mujkanovic, Senahid Cirkic, and Fikret Alic. They beat a group of prisoners in Room 3, including Fahrudin Hrustic, and they beat a group of approximately 18 prisoners confined in Room 2. It was at Keraterm, during the summer of 1992, when the accused Zoran Zigic also brutally beat a prisoner named Jasmin Ramadanovic, known as Sengin. The Keraterm prison camp was also the locale of a bloody massacre of Muslim prisoners from the Brdo region of Prijedor, an area that comprised the villages of Hambarine, Carakavo, Rakovcani, Biscani, and Rizvanovici. Around the 20th of July, 1992, Bosnian Serb forces brought a large number of prisoners from this region to Keraterm and confined them in Room 3, which had been vacated in preparation for the arrival of this particular group of detainees. For days, these men and boys were denied food and water until camp guards, members of the Bosnian Serb army, and visitors to the camp, including the accused Zoran Zigic, finally slaughtered most of them with machine-gun fire. Approximately 200 innocent people were slaughtered that evening in what became known as the Room 3 massacre. The Keraterm camp continued to function until August 6th of 1992. At that time, following the exposure of the camp in the international press, the majority of prisoners were transferred to camps at Trnopolje and Manjaca. The Trnopolje camp. The Trnopolje camp was comprised of a former school, a municipal centre, and a theatre. The majority of the thousands of prisoners held at the Trnopolje camp were elderly people, women and children. The women and girls were often raped, generally during the night when Serb forces arrived and called them out. Generally, there was very little food available and there was almost no drinking water. As at Omarska and Keraterm, the personal hygiene of the prisoners suffered greatly as a result. Disease spread quickly and there was no medical attention provided to those suffering. Dysentery, in particular, was a severe problem. The evidence presented during this trial will prove that inside the Trnopolje camp, during the fateful summer of 1992, the accused Zoran Zigic beat a prisoner named Hasan Karabasic. Many survivors of the horrors of the Omarska and Keraterm prison camps subsequently found themselves in Trnopolje. If we could go to the next document, please. Your Honours, this document is a report in 1993 concerning the Prijedor Public Security Station during the last nine months of 1992, and the relevant section that I'd like to take Your Honours to is a reference to the Trnopolje camp, where, in the words of the report, it's provided that: "The Trnopolje reception centre, however, remained in place until November; in addition to women and children, there was a large concentration of Muslim men fit for military service there, including persons who had spent some time in Omarska and Keraterm because of their direct or indirect involvement in armed rebellion. As several convoys were organised for the transportation of these persons in the direction of Skender Vakuf, Bugojno, Kalovac, and Gradiska, our policemen took part in the escort and security details provided for these convoys." Your Honours, the Trnopolje camp served as a final point of expulsion for many thousands of Muslims and Croats who were forced to leave the Prijedor area. The fortunate souls who survived the brutal conditions of the Prijedor prison camps were bussed by the Bosnian Serb authorities from Trnopolje to other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, often with the cooperation of the Red Cross. If we could look at the next document, please. Your Honours, the document we now see is a translation of a newspaper article, published in Prijedor on the 13th of November, 1992. The article provides: "The unravelling began unexpectedly in the days when the drama of the Trnopolje Reception Centre reached its climax and when the last internees of the centre were literally threatened by death from starvation. Half of the number of internees remain in the centre compared to the number at the end of the last week. "The turning point occurred when the first transit visas arrived in Prijedor from Croatia. Five-hundred passes arrived on Monday alone, and finally the number of the reception centre internees began to decrease. Last week there were 3.200 and it is estimated that the maximum number of internees as of Wednesday is 1.500." And then at the end: "At the reception centre and in the Prijedor municipality, the potential emigrants' agreement is impatiently anticipated, for it would resolve the months-long problem of the Trnopolje Reception Centre. Until then, some 1.500 of its remaining internees continue to starve and freeze." The last prisoners in Trnopolje did not leave the camp until December 1992. May we see the next document, please. Your Honours, this document is an article from the newspaper Lozarski Vjesnik, dated 4 December 1992. It says: "The Trnopolje Reception Centre exists no more. After operating for more than a half a year, and its official closing in mid-October, the reception centre was vacated at around noon of Tuesday. At that moment, there were some 1.560 internees there. Some potential emigrants from the Prijedor municipality returned to their homes and the rest of the internees were housed in some 150 abandoned houses in Donja Ljubija." In September 1992, Milomir Stakic, president of the Prijedor Municipality, explained why the prisoners from Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje camps were moved. Could we go to the next document, please. Your Honours, this document is an extract from the minutes of the meeting of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly of September 1992, and the relevant part of that document, if we could see it on the screen, please, is marked with the blue there, Your Honours. It reads: "Stakic indicated that two key reasons which had motivated the cabinet in Pale to make such a decision: The pressure from the international public opinion and official policy, and the steep cost of maintaining the prisons." Your Honours, this document is also one of those documents that provides proof of the chain of command and lines of authority that existed between the Bosnian Serb government and Dr. Radovan Karadzic based in Pale, and the ongoing persecution campaign against Muslims and Croats in Prijedor. These prison camps were an integral component of the Bosnian Serb persecution machine. Of course, there were no guarantees that prisoners who survived the horrors of these detention camps would survive the expulsion process. On the 21st of August 1992, in a remote region known as the Koricani Cliffs, a large number of prisoners were murdered in cold blood after they had been removed by bus and truck from the Trnopolje Camp. Ostensibly, they were being transferred from Trnopolje to a Muslim-held part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This incident, Your Honours, became widely known, and when this became widely known, the Bosnian Serb authorities in Banja Luka were spurred into taking official action and, subsequently, acknowledged that approximately 150 Muslims were killed at the Koricani Cliffs. Could I have the next document, please. You'll see in this document, Your Honours, that it is an order from the ARK chief of police Stojan Zupljanin, the superior of Simo Drljaca, who was referred to. This is an order that he's sending to Simo Drljaca: "I order you to conduct a full investigation in accordance with the laws and other regulations of the killing of about 150 Muslim people in the area of Skender Vakuf municipality. "You will inform the Ministry immediately about the results of this investigation, and in the case that the above-mentioned allegation is confirmed, you will start legal proceedings against the perpetrators. "Minister Mico Stansic. "In connection with this order, it is necessary to immediately take written statements about the events at Skender Vakuf from the policemen that escorted the convoy from Prijedor to the border of Travnik on 21 August 1992." It's signed by Stojan Zupljanin. However, the perpetrators of this crime were far less intimidated by such things as international public opinion. Consequently, the requested investigation never occurred. Simo Drljaca, the police chief in Prijedor, arrogantly informed his superiors that the policemen who escorted the convoy on 21 August 1992 were on combat duty and, consequently, unavailable to cooperate with the investigators. If we can look, please at the next document. This is his reply to his superior in Banja Luka, where he says: "In response to your dispatch, number and date of communication, we inform you that we're not able to conduct an investigation regarding the alleged death of a number of Muslims in the area of Koricanske stijene, since all of the policemen who were involved in the escort of the Travnik convoy on 21 August 1992 have been deployed on the Hans Pijesak front since 9 September, 1992. "Also, we are unable to provide you with the lists of the citizens who travelled on those convoys, since the public security station did not organise those convoys but only assigned a certain number of policemen to the duty of providing physical security for the convoy as required by the army and the Red Cross." It's signed by Simo Drljaca. The accused. The accused in this trial and the prison camps in Prijedor where three of the four accused were employed were an integral component of the violent campaign of persecution which Bosnian Serb leaders orchestrated in north-western Bosnia during 1992. Allow me to provide you with more specific information about these accused and the conduct of each of them in the camps in Prijedor. The accused Miroslav Kvocka was born on January 1, 1957 in the village of Maricka, in the Prijedor municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Prior to the armed conflict, he was a police officer in the Prijedor municipality. Kvocka was the first camp commander at Omarska. In June 1992, he was replaced in that position by Zeljko Meakic. At that time, Mr. Kvocka became the Deputy Commander of the camp. The accused Kvocka was present at the Omarska camp daily and often demonstrated that he was in control. When Zeljko Meakic was not present in the camp, Kvocka would receive important Serb visitors. Due to the positions he held, first as Commander and later Deputy Commander, the accused Kvocka was in a position of superior authority to everyone in the camp except Zeljko Meakic when he was present. The accused Milojica Kos, also known as "Krle," was born on April 1, 1963, in the village of Lamovita in the Prijedor municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Before the outbreak break of the conflict in the region, he was a reserve policeman attached to the Omarska police station. Mr. Kos acted as one of the three guard shift commanders at Omarska, and in that capacity he supervised a number of guards. As a shift commander, Kos was subordinate only to the camp commander Zeljko Meakic and the Deputy Commander, the accused Kvocka. Each shift of guards was comprised of approximately 30 men. While the accused Kos was on duty at Omarska, he had command and control over every guard on his shift and, therefore, was in a position of superior authority to them. The accused Mladjo Radic, also known as "Krkan," was born on May 15, 1952, also in the village of Lamovita in the Prijedor municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Prior to the outbreak of the conflict, the accused Radic was a police officer in the Prijedor municipality and worked out of the Omarska police station. Radic was one of the three guard shift commanders at Omarska. His position as shift commander meant that he was subordinate only to the accused Kvocka and the commander of the camp, Zeljko Meakic. Like the accused Kos, Radic was in a position of superior authority to all of the guards on his shift. The accused Zoran Zigic. Zoran Zigic was born on September 20, 1958 in the village of Balte in the Prijedor municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Prior to the armed conflict he was a taxi driver. He did not hold a formal position at any of the camps but entered all three of them periodically for the purpose of beating, torturing, murdering, harassing, and robbing prisoners. The evidence presented during this trial will prove beyond reasonable doubt that each of the accused bear individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Tribunal's Statute for serious violations of International Humanitarian Law at the Omarska camp between May 24th and August 30th, 1992. Additionally, the evidence will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that all of the accused, with the exception of Zoran Zigic, were responsible under Article 7(3) for the criminal acts of their subordinates at the Omarska camp during the relevant period during the amended indictment. The evidence will prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused Kvocka, Kos, and Radic knew or had reason to know that their subordinates were about to commit such criminal acts or had done so and failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish them. In order to understand the discriminatory nature of these crimes committed by these accused, it's necessary to understand the political environment in which they occurred and which led to the creation of the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje prison camps. The Serbian Democratic Party, also known as the SDS, was founded in the summer of 1992, sorry, 1990, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, the SDS adopted a programme and statutes and elected Dr. Radovan Karadzic as its president. Shortly thereafter, SDS leaders began to openly advocate the formation of a Greater Serbia. In September of 1991, Bosnian Serb leaders proclaimed the establishment of several Serb autonomous regions, with the aim of separating from the republican government agencies in Sarajevo and creating a Greater Serbia. Prijedor was located within the Bosanska Krajina. And if I may be assisted, could we have the map, please. Looking at the map, Your Honours, the arrow now pointing indicates the opstina or the municipality of Prijedor and that town, and we can see relatively closely to it the town of Banja Luka. The autonomous region consisted of the city of Banja Luka and the surrounding municipalities where the Serbs constituted a clear majority. Several of the municipalities that the SDS leadership had planned on joining the autonomous region, including Prijedor, didn't, in fact, join it in 1991. This left Prijedor virtually isolated, surrounded by other municipalities that had joined the Serb association. Thank you. Bosnian Serb deputies of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina took another step towards the creation of Greater Serbia when they established the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 24th of October of 1991. That assembly was the highest organ of the political party in the SDS. On the 9th of January, 1992, Bosnian Serb leaders proclaimed the creation of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 26th of January 1992, the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted its constitutional resolution. If we could have the next document, please. Your Honours, this document is an extract of the minutes of the Assembly of the Republic of the Bosnian Serb People of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 26th of January 1992. If I could just take Your Honours to a number of the paragraphs of that document. Paragraph 3: "The Assembly of the Serbian People of the Bosnia and Herzegovina hereby task the Ministerial Council, working bodies, and other authorised representatives of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina to draft the constitution, relevant decisions, and other instruments which would regulate, as soon as possible, the subsequent organisation of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state so that the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina can function as an actual state entity." Paragraph 4: "The place of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina is in a common state of the Serbian people. The democratic transformation of Yugoslavia must be conducted parallel with the organisation of the entire Serbian people into a Serbian Federation or a union of Serbian states." And finally: "It's necessary immediately to redefine our relationship with Yugoslav federal institutions, in particular with the JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, on the basis of our mutual, political and existential interests." SDS leaders justified their action by the results of a rigged plebiscite that purported to show overwhelming popular support for the inclusion of Bosnia and Herzegovina into a federal Yugoslavia. Could we have the next document, please. At a meeting of the SDS Prijedor Municipal Board in February 1992, an SDS leader named Srdo Srdic noted that: "An important argument for our transformation is the plebiscite we conducted. The creation of states brings about a mass emigration and the resettlement and the exchange of territories which is imminent." In early 1992, SDS and military forces in the region began to establish parallel municipal governments and separate police forces in areas like Prijedor. The SDS president, Radovan Karadzic, reiterated the Bosnian Serbian push towards the creation of a Serbian state at the same SDS meeting at Prijedor. If we could have the next document. He explained to a gathering of the SDS leaders that: "We are forced to create national communities on ethnic territories. There will be a maximum strengthening of authority in the regions (economically and politically) and the activities of the region of Bosnian Krajina are geared towards that. After the situation in the country calmed down and the pre-conditions are there, the will of the people would bring about the unification of all Serb territories and communities." In March 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina promulgated the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and declared itself a distinct republic. During that spring, Bosnian Serbs took control of the television tower on Kozara Mountain, which ensured that the residents of Prijedor municipality could only receive programmes from Belgrade or Novi Sad in Serbia and Pale and Banja Luka in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Television was a powerful medium through which the Bosnian Serb leaders could disseminate racist and inflammatory propaganda. Throughout this period, symbols of Serbian nationalism, including flags, songs, and emblems became prevalent as well. On April 30, 1992, the SDS conducted a bloodless takeover of Prijedor town with the assistance of the military and police forces. Could we have a look at the next document, please. This document is a dispatch issued by the Prijedor Public Security Station on the date of the takeover and provides us with many of the details about that event. In part, it provides, for example, that: "Ten police stations, numbering 1.587 members, were mobilised. All call-ups were responded to and there was no avoidance of work obligations. At 0400 hours, in keeping with the conclusions reached by the executive committee of the Serbian Assembly of the Prijedor municipality, power was taken over in the territory of the municipality when possession was taken of all public security stations and other strategic points. These activities were carried out in synchronised action and not a single bullet was fired. The normal work and functioning of the service was ensured by organising security guards and patrols. Economic and non-economic organisations are operating normally. We shall inform you in due time about our future activities. Signed Simo Drljaca." The SDS leaders in Prijedor were instructed to take control of every aspect of municipal government, and they acted in concert with the army of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the JNA. The late Milan Kovacevic described the takeover of the Prijedor municipality in an interview on Radio Prijedor in 1995. If we could have a look at this document, please. In a relevant part of the document, he describes the takeover in the following terms: "It was all neatly prepared and done, and we waited for the moment which we had set, and then on today's date, 0400 hours, a few years ago, we did it. To my and many other people's surprise, it really went the way we had planned. I mean, they told me that from SUP, that is to say, from the centre, Simo and the others told me that they had announced from our staff that the movement would begin, and in 28 minutes I was at the post of the chairman of the Executive Board, and Stakic was at the post of the president of the Municipal Assembly. All bodies of authority were in place and began functioning from that moment on ..." So some kind of transition was made from those national parties, today opinions may vary, but those were, indeed, national parties and it's good that they were. "So twenty minutes after the departure from Cirkin Polje municipality, bodies resumed their work as if nothing had happened. That was done without casualties or shooting. Nothing. We just came to our respective offices and began working, as if it had been like that for centuries and thank God it still goes on ..." Your Honours, over 1.500 people were mobilised, organised, and deployed in the efficient Serbian takeover of Prijedor. This was a well-planned, highly coordinated operation between police, politicians, and military authorities. By the end of April 1992, the Bosnian Serbs had taken control of the Prijedor municipality and renamed it the "Serbian Prijedor municipality." That signalled the intensification of the Bosnian Serbs' campaign of persecution of the Muslims and Croats in the Prijedor municipality in order to eliminate them from the area. The Bosnian Serb authorities had important strategic reasons for executing their campaign of persecution against non-Serbs in Prijedor. The municipality of Prijedor lies in the Krajina region, "Krajina" meaning border-region, of north-western Bosnia. It is located along one of the major travel corridors running east to west in the former Yugoslavia. If we could have the map again, please. As Your Honour sees the cursor moving along, it runs through that area and down the Krajina border, or the border which had a large occupation of Serbian people. As such, it was invaluable to the Bosnian Serb leaders aspiring to create their Greater Serbia, because it served as a link between the Serb-dominated Croatian Krajina to the west of the republic and to the Republic of Serbia to the east. The ultimate goal of Bosnian Serb political leaders was to integrate the entire Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, including the Prijedor municipality, into Greater Serbia. If we could see the next document, please. Your Honours, this document is the extract of minutes of the meeting of the SDS Municipal Board of Prijedor in December of 1991, and Milan Kovacevic says in the relevant part: "Prijedor is the most important district in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are in a war situation, which makes our work more difficult ... This is a moment critical for the survival of the Serbian people, especially in BH." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, is it possible for you, when it is convenient for you, to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. So we will have a break of 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have planned to continue until 3.30, Mr. Niemann. I'm telling you that for you to be able to manage the time. We're going to work for one hour, twenty; then we'll have a break. So I give you the floor. You may continue, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, Serb authority in Prijedor and other parts of north-west Bosnia was consolidated under the Crisis Headquarters of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, or the ARK Crisis Staff. This institution was also known as the ARK War Staff. In early May of 1992, the ARK Crisis Staff, headquartered in the city of Banja Luka, took over all powers of government and municipal crisis staffs, such as that established in Prijedor, and implemented its decision. For example, there was intense pressure for the Bosnian Serb men to respond to the call for mobilisation. Can I have the next document, please. On the 10th of June, 1992, the ARK Crisis Staff adopted a decision that stated that "Only children, women, and old men may emigrate from the Autonomous Region of Krajina if they so wish." Thank you. Bosnian Serb men, quite obviously, were expected to fight for the Serb cause. Muslim and Croat men, who might return one day to fight for their homes, could not be permitted to leave the area. In June of 1992, the Prijedor Crisis Staff issued a set of detailed instructions on the establishment, composition, and tasks of the local crisis staff in the Prijedor municipality. Could we have the next document, please. The basic duties of the local crisis staff, according to these instructions, was as follows: "to exercise and coordinate authority in the local territory; to maintain effective protection and defence of the local territory and secure all prerequisites essential for successful armed combat; to control the security of the territory, protect the safety of citizens and their property as well as the safety of socially-owned property, ensuring consistent adherence to the existing regulations; to maintain constant synchronisation and coordination of the measures and actions of the military and the police in the local area; to organise and implement preventive and operative civil protection measures; to develop the most varied forms and methods of information and political propaganda activities; to organise and revive the economy, especially agriculture (sowing, harvesting, threshing, mowing, and the gathering of other agricultural produce) and organise the buy-up of the agricultural produce; to organise supplies including the provision of transport and technical means; to organise medical services and care for the wounded and the sick; to organise suitable help for the families of dead combatants." These instructions gave the local crisis staff a wide range of duties and, obviously, a great deal of power. The municipal crisis staffs such as that of Prijedor had to provide daily reports to the ARK Crisis Staff regarding steps taken to implement the discriminatory policies of the Main Board located in Banja Luka. After the Bosnian Serb takeover of Prijedor on 30 April 1992, conditions for the Bosnian Muslims and Croats in the Prijedor municipality deteriorated rapidly. Prominent members of the Muslim and Croat community, particularly members of the SDA, the leading Muslim political party, and the HDZ, the leading Croat political party, were dismissed from their jobs and subjected to harassment. If we could have the next document, please. This document, these are the minutes of a meeting of the Prijedor Municipal Board of the SDS on 9 May 1992, which reflect the onset of discriminatory policies and practices that foreshadowed the widespread ethnic cleansing campaign to come. At the meeting, Milan Kovacevic, the President of the Municipal Assembly Executive Committee said: "The cabinet meets daily and has adopted at least 50 decisions, the most important of which include: replacement of staff has been carried out, with all SDA leaders removed from functions in the Municipal Assembly; the functioning of government at the level of Krajina can now be felt; instructions and decisions are being forwarded from the top; larger companies and institutions have separated themselves from Sarajevo; financial transactions have resumed; the cabinet will continue to meet constantly; all measures, decisions, and conclusions must be verified by the Assembly; local boards of the SDS must be more active." Thank you. The expulsion of Muslims and Croats from the Prijedor region became a priority of the Bosnian Serb authorities. Could we have the next document, please. On 26 May 1992, just four days before the police chief of Prijedor issued his orders concerning the establishment and functioning of the Omarska camp, the ARK Crisis Staff issued a series of orders, and among them, we have order 5 [as read]: "5. A committee shall be formed for negotiations with members of other nationalities and representatives of Herceg-Bosna. "6. An agency shall be established that will work on the problem of population resettlement." Your Honours, as you review these documents and consider the testimony of the victims of this case, I hope that you will look beyond the rather clinical language used in the documents such as to mask the true nature of the Bosnian Serb plans and policies. The Prosecution will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the Bosnian Serb solution to the so-called "problem of population emigration" was a widespread, systematic, and violent campaign of ethnic cleansing designed to kill or expel the majority of ethnic Muslims and Croats in Prijedor. The enormity of this criminal task eventually required the active participation and coordination of several agencies of government, including the military, the police, and the municipal and regional crisis staffs. Prior to the armed conflict, the JNA 5th Corps, headquartered in Banja Luka, was the predominant military power in the Prijedor region. As of 19 May 1992, when the JNA supposedly departed from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the name of the 5th Corps of the JNA changed to the 1st Krajina Corps of the Republika Srpska army. However, the same commanding general and Serb officer corps remained in control. That military unit was responsible for ordering the deployment of artillery and troops on the hills surrounding the town of Kozarac, a predominantly Muslim town near the city of Prijedor. The Bosnian Serbs justified the start of violent expulsions of Muslims and Croats from their homes in the Prijedor municipality with the pretext of an attack against Serbs. Next document, please. In a dispatch dated the 26th of May, 1992, Simo Drljaca advised his superiors in Banja Luka of the events in Prijedor: "We hereby notify you that the fighting which began on 22 May 1992 with the killing and wounding of a group of military reservists is still continuing on the territory of Prijedor municipality. A mopping-up operation is currently underway on the territory of Kozarac, Kozarusa, Kamicani, and the Trnopolje local communities." Further on, he says: "In other Muslim-populated peripheral areas of the municipality, as well as in the town itself, sporadic small-arms fire can be heard from time to time, although the weapons are being handed over in an organised way and are being seized during searches of apartments and other buildings ..." He then goes on: "Further activities in this connection will be carried out in an organised way and in cooperation with the military authorities and members of the National Security Service." Your Honours, the military attacks were carried out by the combined forces of the 1st Krajina Corps of the Bosnian Serb army, army reservists from Prijedor, regular and reserve police officers from Prijedor, and paramilitary units organised and equipped by the SDS. There was a pattern to these operations as huge quantities of artillery were first used to shell the non-Serb neighbourhoods in order to quash any resistance. Your Honours, these weren't military targets, these were the homes of civilians, the homes of civilians who, in most cases, happened to be Muslims. If we may see some of the results of this military campaign on the Muslim town of Prijedor -- Kozarac, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is the town of Kozarac, as we move up the main street of the town, where the shops are and the local houses are, mostly of Muslim people, who were forced out of their homes and into the camps. Some of the buildings are untouched. Generally, in those cases, those buildings belonged to the Serbs. Such was the meticulous nature of the campaign where only the Muslim properties were destroyed. With such destruction, people had nowhere to go. But not only were their homes attacked and destroyed, but also their religious monuments. It could hardly be a military target, but the mosque that you now see appearing was destroyed and gutted. That was one side of the road. This is the other, going back down the centre of the town of Kozarac. As I said, the religious monuments were also attacked, but not the Serbian religious monuments such as this Serbian Orthodox Church in Kozarac. Your Honours, following these attacks, the Serb paramilitary groups systematically rounded up ethnic Muslims and Croats, and expelled the non-Serb population from the area. Those who evaded captured fled to the surrounding mountains and forests. Once captured, most of the women and children were taken to the Trnopolje Camp. The men, on the other hand, were usually taken to Omarska or Keraterm. Oftentimes, civilians were interrogated at the Prijedor police station and then subsequently transferred to Omarska or to the other prison camps. Could we have the next document, please. This is an extract from the newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik of 19 November 1993, and we see in the relevant section of this article the following: "Following the armed uprising, reception centres were set up in Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje, where officers of the SJB (police station) were taking people in for questioning, carrying out operative processing and security operations." The Bosnian Serb authorities, including the accused sitting before you, confined Muslim and Croat civilians for a variety of highly dubious and artificial reasons. One justification for confinement was a familial relationship to a Muslim political leader. Can we see the next document, please. For example, in a note from the Prijedor police station, one official wrote: "Since Kapetanovic is Muhamed Cehajic's brother-in-law, there are grounds for believing that he has been aware of the illegal activities of the SDA. "This information indicated involvement in white-collar crime and bribes-taking, as well as his nationalistic attitude towards officials of Serbian nationality. Therefore, a further processing at Omarska location is recommended." Your Honours, you'll note that the term "processing" crops up rather frequently in these documents. The term "processing" had a special significance in Prijedor during the summer of 1992. For example, Muhamed Cehajic, the man referred to in the document you've just seen, was a Muslim, and, prior to the armed conflict, the president of the Prijedor Executive Board, a position roughly equivalent to the mayor of a town in other parts of the world. He is also a victim, specifically named in the schedules to the amended indictment. During the course of this trial, you'll hear testimony describing how Muhamed Cehajic was seen in the administrative building at Omarska camp, covered with bruises, and how Mr. Cehajic was taken away on or about the 26th of July 1992 and was never seen again. Often, Muslim members of the SDA were arrested because they were considered to be extremists who posed a threat to the fledgling Serbian state because of their political views. The next document, please. According to one police intelligence report from Prijedor compiled in July 1992, it says: "At number 6 in II Krajiske Brigade Street, the extremist Enes Kadiric is staying in a house owned by Muharem Kadiric. He is an important member of the SDA in the organisation in the village of Biscani, where he is hiding in the house of his above-named relative. Therefore, the arrest of both Muharem Dadiric and Enes Kadiric should be effected on the grounds of suspicion, and it is true that both are extremists and pose a threat to the present system of government. According to information volunteered by Dragoja Rodic, a year ago when he was working as a production manager, he, Kadiric, dismissed Serbian staff, claiming that there would be no room for them in what today is the Krajina if they did not convert to Islam." Then further on in the document there is an addendum. It says: "Enes is much more extremist than the note conveys. In the Oslobodenje branch office he got rid of each and every Serb and harassed them, employing Turks as he pleased. I am not going to do a lot of writing here, but for what he has done so far, death is all he deserves to have from the Serbs." Finally, at the top right-hand corner of the very same document, you will see a note from Dragoljub Mudrinic, who added another directive: "Check the statement in this note and take appropriate measures in order to process and arrest. 23 July 1992." Your Honours, by July 28th, Mr. Enes Kadiric was in the custody of the Bosnian Serb authorities and his processing had begun. Additionally, the Banja Luka Public Security Station was collecting intelligence information on Muslims who were in possession of weapons and who were allegedly organising themselves against the Bosnian Serbs. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal now describes three distinct categories of collective criminality that fall within the doctrine of the common purpose liability. During the course of the trial, you will hear evidence that speaks to each of these three categories, so permit me now to take a moment to review each category and its relevance to these four accused. The first category includes those cases where all perpetrators, acting pursuant to a common design, possess the same criminal intention, although their methods of participation may differ. For example, our Appeals Chamber cited the decision rendered in the Einsatzgruppen case, where a Nuremberg tribunal noted that guilt for murder is not restricted to the man who pulls the trigger or buries the corpse. That tribunal said: "Thus, not only are principals guilty but also accessories, those who take a consenting part in the commission of crime or are connected with plans or enterprises involved in its commission, those who order or abet crime, and those who belong to an organisation or group engaged in the commission of crime." That is quoted, Your Honours, at paragraph 200 of the Tadic Appeals Judgement. With regard to the actus reus and mens rea, the Tadic Appeals Chamber defined two criteria for liability under this first category of the common purpose doctrine. First, the accused must voluntarily participate in one aspect of the common design, and second, the accused, even if not personally effecting the criminal act, must nevertheless intend its result. Whenever Zigic came to the camp, he would select a few prisoners and take them out of the White House for beatings. We sitting on the pista could hear the screams and beatings of these prisoners. They would be beaten while the doors of the White House would be closed. "On one such occasion, I saw Kvocka speaking to a guard near the entrance of the restaurant. At that moment, Zoran Zigic came and called out Asef, Kiki, and Began. I don't know the names of Began and Kiki. As Zigic was calling out these names, the guards said to the prisoners on the pista to lay on the floor facing the ground. Soon after, we heard the screams and there is no way Kvocka could not have heard it. We were facing the floor for at least three hours, and during most of that time we could hear screams and cries coming from the direction of the White House." All of the accused in this proceeding shared the common criminal design to persecute Muslims and Croats in Prijedor so as to cleanse the region of those who would not participate in their Serbian state. In the Tadic Appeals Judgement, the Appeals Chamber concluded that criminal responsibility may be imputed to all participants within a common enterprise when the risk of injury occurring was both a predictable consequence of the execution of the common design and the accused was either reckless or indifferent to that task. The evidence during this trial, such as the testimony of (redacted), will describe a calculated acquiescence by camp superiors to the violent acts of persons such as the accused Zigic and his associates. These visits happened so often, so openly, and with such predictable brutality that the injuries inflicted on the victims in this proceeding can never be confused with mere coincidence. Therefore, under the third category of common design liability, by permitting the entrance of accused Zoran Zigic and others like him into the Omarska camp, and by doing nothing to present such incursions, the accused Kvocka, Radic, and Kos, also became responsible for the natural, foreseeable, and horrible consequence of these events. Under the third category of common purpose liability, the criminal responsibility of these three men in authority rests on the manifest of recklessness or indifference or both, which these three demonstrated in the face of the predictable dangers created by the presence of men like Zoran Zigic within this camp. The four accused, therefore, did not all participate in the common design to persecute Muslims and Croats in exactly the same manner, but it was the composite of the actions of all that resulted in the commission of these crimes which lie at the heart of these proceedings. Your Honours, the evidence presented during this trial will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that this group of men shared a common purpose to rid the Prijedor area of Muslims and Croats. Many of the victims arrived in the prison camps after being detained during military or paramilitary ethic cleansing operations in the areas where they resided, their homes. Each of the accused actively participated in this common design, and in so doing, each bears responsibility for the crimes against humanity and violations of the laws of war. 7(3), authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, Mr. Niemann. Perhaps before going on to this point it would be convenient to have a break. What do you think about it, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm happy to do what would suit Your Honours, but I have four pages to go. If you would like to hear me complete, I can conclude it in four pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that all for the opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it would be better to make a little extra effort and to finish with your opening statement. So you may continue, Mr. Niemann. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was going on, Your Honours, to mention Article 7(3), authority. All of the accused, except for Zoran Zigic, are also or alternatively criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates with respect to the crimes charged in the indictment by virtue of their respective positions of superior authority in the camps, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Article 7(3) defines a person in a position of superior authority as one who is responsible for the criminal acts of his subordinates if the superior knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit such acts or had done so and the superior failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the subordinates. In the Celebici judgement, the Trial Chamber articulated that Article 7(3) not only includes the responsibility of military commanders but also the responsibility of civilian authorities. This is paragraph 343 to 363. The evidence presented in this trial will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Kvocka, Radic, and Kos, exercised effective control over their subordinate guards at the Omarska prison camp. Your Honours, the Prosecution will submit evidence concerning the continuing effects of ethic cleansing on the lives of the surviving Muslim and Croat victims from Prijedor even to this day. This evidence will assist the Trial Chamber in determining the appropriate sentence if one or more of the four accused are found guilty of the charges in the amendment indictment. In our submission, Your Honours, this evidence is admissible under Rule 84(A)(vi) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As you are aware, the parties have agreed that following the presentation of the opening statement, some of the accused will testify. However, the use of this procedure will not relieve the Prosecution of its burden of proving each and every element of the charges beyond a reasonable doubt. Accordingly, following the testimony of those accused, the Prosecution will present its case with the vigour, thoroughness, and independence mandated by the Statute of the Tribunal. Your Honours, the Prosecution expects to call a number of witnesses and has already presented documentary exhibits to the Trial Chamber. Some footage and photographs will be introduced as well. The Prosecution evidence will prove the culpability of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. In the interests of justice, they must be held, in our submission, accountable for their criminal behaviour. The International Community demands that these heinous crimes be exposed and punished according to international law. Accordingly, Your Honours, at the close of these proceedings, the Prosecution will ask you to find each of the accused guilty as charged. Unless I can assist Your Honours with any other matter, that is my opening address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Mr. Niemann. I think we have before us plenty of time to clear up all the points that you have presented to us. I think that the Defence of Mr. Kos would like to say something and, therefore, I should give the floor to his Defence counsel. Mr. Nikolic, please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, the Defence of the accused Kos would, first of all, like to tender its apologies for what we are going to say now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nikolic. I didn't hear the beginning of your statement. Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be glad to. Your Honours, the Defence of the accused Mr. Kos would, first of all, like to tender its apologies for what we are now going to say, because the Defence is aware of the efforts you have invested in scheduling this trial. I appeal to you to accept this request and to treat it as the right of the accused to seek out the best method of defending himself, and as his Defence counsel, I am simply conveying to you his position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that all? You may be seated, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, we have a question for you. What you have just told us is the renunciation of the right to testify now, or after, throughout the trial, or is the accused just renouncing this right for the beginning of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, only as regards the opening of the trial.
